page_hint: Chapter 11, §3 When to Disaggregate and Fig 11.3 note
quoted_clause: at batch size 1 and 25 ms TPOT — 40 tokens/s — the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host, Ch 6; batching divides the rate proportionally
observed: The decode-bandwidth wording conflates required per-step HBM traffic with available HBM bandwidth, and it says batching divides the whole-model weight-read rate. In autoregressive decode, the weights are read once per step for the whole batch, so at fixed TPOT the per-step whole-model weight-read requirement is approximately independent of batch size; batching increases total token rate and reduces per-token weight-read cost, not the per-step whole-model read rate. The same issue appears in §3, where 3.35 TB/s is listed as if it were a weight-read rate rather than the H100 HBM ceiling.
evidence: 140 GB / 0.025 s = 5.6 TB/s per step if unsharded. With 8-way TP, 140/8 = 17.5 GB per GPU, and 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 0.70 TB/s per GPU per step. H100 HBM bandwidth is 3.35 TB/s per GPU (Table 9-1), not a required weight-read rate. Increasing batch from 1 to 17.5 changes token rate from 40 tok/s to about 700 tok/s while the per-step weight-read requirement remains about 5.6 TB/s unsharded or 0.70 TB/s per GPU sharded.
root_cause: Per-step HBM traffic, available HBM bandwidth, and per-token amortized cost are not kept distinct.
correction: In both locations, rewrite to distinguish required versus available bandwidth and per-step versus per-token cost. For example: 'the required whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6 TB/s if unsharded, against 3.35 TB/s per GPU of HBM bandwidth, and ~0.70 TB/s per GPU when sharded across the canonical 8×H100 host; batching divides the per-token weight-read cost, not the per-step whole-model weight-read rate at fixed TPOT.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Chapter 11 lists 3.35 TB/s as a required weight-read rate, and no sentence implies that the per-step whole-model HBM weight-read bandwidth decreases as batch size increases at fixed TPOT.

quoted_clause: This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand
observed: The generic rule 'throughput per device multiplied by number of devices' is inconsistent with tensor-parallel aggregation. Earlier in the same chapter, an 8×H100 TP=8 host is said to sustain about 19,800 prefill tokens/s total, not 8 times the per-GPU shared-stream rate. A single device's token rate can be summed across devices for data-parallel replicas, but not for TP/PP layouts where the token stream is shared across the group.
evidence: Candidate (a) states: 'each GPU carries ~19,780 tok/s of the shared token stream ... so the host aggregate is the same ~19,800 — not 8× a per-GPU rate.' The §4 rule, however, says the per-device number is multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, which would imply 8 × 19,780 for a TP=8 host.
root_cause: Capacity aggregation is presented as a single device-count multiplication without separating DP from TP/PP token-stream accounting.
correction: Replace the multiplication rule with a parallelism-aware rule: 'For DP, sum the per-replica rates. For TP/PP, use the layout's token-stream accounting; an 8×H100 TP=8 host is not 8× the per-GPU full-model or shared-stream rate (see Candidate (a)).'
acceptance_test: No capacity formula in Chapter 12 implies that a TP=8 host's prefill token rate is 8× the per-GPU shared-stream rate.

quoted_clause: If the architecture calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE.
observed: The sentence can be read as assuming a feasible plain data-parallel training deployment of a 70B FP16 model with one rank per node/GPU. Plain DP requires each rank to hold the full 140 GB model plus training state, which does not fit an 80 GB H100. The chapter and Chapter 10 explicitly say the 140 GB weight tensor does not fit one 80 GB GPU and that plain DP is infeasible for the canonical 70B on H100.
evidence: Chapter 9 §3: 'Neither a 140 GB weight tensor nor this gradient buffer fits on one 80 GB GPU.' Chapter 10 §3: 'Plain data parallelism is infeasible here: it would replicate the 140 GB model on every GPU, and at 80 GB HBM per H100 the replica does not fit on one device.'
root_cause: Missing qualification that the DP all-reduce example is communication-only or that each DP rank is backed by a multi-GPU node / sharded DP layout.
correction: Reword to make the feasibility assumption explicit, e.g. 'If the architecture models an eight-rank DP all-reduce for a 70B FP16 training job (communication-only, or with each rank backed by an 8-GPU node / sharded DP), the inter-node all-reduce bandwidth dictates ...' or 'one rank per 8-GPU node' instead of 'one rank per node' if rank means GPU.
acceptance_test: The sentence does not imply that a single H100 rank can hold a full 70B FP16 training replica.

quoted_clause: MoE models (if chosen per Ch3) push toward EP, because the full expert set must be resident (the active count sets compute per token, not residency) and EP shards the experts across GPUs.
observed: The clause states that the full expert set must be resident as a general reason for using EP. Expert offloading, caching, or non-resident expert storage can change the residency requirement. The same chapter later qualifies this point in §7, so the unqualified statement in the architecture-consequence section is inconsistent with the more careful later treatment.
evidence: Chapter 10 §7 says: 'the total expert residency that must be sharded if the deployment keeps all experts resident in HBM (expert offloading or caching otherwise changes the capacity calculus).'
root_cause: The summary bullet omits the residency assumption that is present in the uncertainty section.
correction: Add scope: 'when the deployment keeps the full expert set resident in HBM; expert offloading or caching changes the residency calculus (see §7).'
acceptance_test: The MoE bullet does not assert full expert residency as unconditional.

quoted_clause: each per-layer all-reduce operates on a ~256 KiB logical tensor — batch × hidden × bytes — so an 8-rank ring sends 1.75 × that ≈ 0.45 MB per rank; across all 80 layers the per-step total is ~36 MB of per-rank send traffic, against ~20 MB of logical volume, sub-MB to tens of MB and not GBs at the canonical batch and hidden size
observed: This mini-case uses one 256 KiB all-reduce per layer and calls the result canonical. Chapter 10's TP decode budget uses two 256 KiB all-reduces per transformer block (attention output and MLP), giving 70 MiB per rank per step, roughly double the Chapter 9 figure. Also, 256 KiB corresponds to 16 sequences, while the canonical decode concurrency used elsewhere is about 17.5.
evidence: Chapter 10 §3: 'Assume two output all-reduces per transformer block — attention output and MLP — 80 blocks ... Across 160 calls ... each rank sends 70 MiB and receives 70 MiB in that one decode step.' Chapter 11 §3: 'canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point.'
root_cause: A simplified one-collective-per-layer, 16-sequence example is presented as canonical without aligning it to Chapter 10's two-collective assumption or the canonical concurrency.
correction: Either label the Chapter 9 example as 'simplified one-collective-per-layer, 16-sequence illustrative' or update it to two collectives per block and/or 17.5 sequences, with a cross-reference to Chapter 10's TP decode budget.
acceptance_test: Chapter 9 mini-case and Chapter 10 TP decode example either match or explicitly state different assumptions.

quoted_clause: model fits one GPU; need throughput
observed: The 'Fits when' cell for data parallelism can be read as requiring the full model to fit one GPU for any DP use. Plain DP does require that, but DP is commonly composed with TP/PP when the model does not fit one device. The chapter's own canonical 70B uses TP=8 within each DP replica, so the table cell is too narrow if read as a general DP condition.
evidence: Chapter 10 §6: 'The canonical 70B fits across an 8×H100 node through intra-host model parallelism; additional replicas address fleet capacity.' The table footnote says the canonical 70B exceeds one H100, so DP is not its baseline, but the cell still says 'model fits one GPU.'
root_cause: The table compresses plain-DP feasibility into a general DP condition without noting composition with TP/PP.
correction: Change the cell to 'plain DP (without TP/PP): full model fits one device; DP can be composed with TP/PP for larger models' or add a table note.
acceptance_test: A reader does not conclude that DP is unavailable for a 70B simply because the model does not fit one H100.

quoted_clause: the decode pool runs bandwidth-saturated on the 300 output tokens
observed: 'Bandwidth-saturated' can mean HBM bandwidth is near its maximum. At the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 decode operating point, the sharded weight-read requirement is about 0.70 TB/s per GPU, well below the 3.35 TB/s HBM ceiling. Decode is bandwidth-bound in the roofline sense, not necessarily saturated.
evidence: Chapter 11 §3 gives the sharded decode weight-read rate as ~0.70 TB/s per GPU, and Table 9-1 gives H100 HBM bandwidth as 3.35 TB/s per GPU.
correction: Reword to 'the decode pool runs bandwidth-bound (not necessarily HBM-saturated) on the 300 output tokens.'
acceptance_test: No sentence claims the canonical decode pool uses near-100% HBM bandwidth.

observed: The table column headed 'SLO' contains memory checks, phase-split capability, and quality status, not only SLO/latency compliance. This blurs the three gates (memory fit, throughput at the SLO, quality) and can make readers think memory and quality are SLO items.
evidence: Row (a) SLO cell: '✓ memory 164 < 640 GB · ? TTFT SLO unmeasured'; row (b): '✓ memory per host · ✓ phase-split enables independent scaling'; row (c): '✗ quality — provisional.'
root_cause: Column label is too narrow for mixed gate status.
correction: Rename the column to 'Gate status' or split it into 'Memory', 'Throughput/SLO', and 'Quality' columns consistent with the table title.
acceptance_test: Table 12-1 column headers accurately describe the content; the SLO column contains only latency/SLO compliance or is renamed.

page_hint: Chapter 10, §7 What We Still Don't Know, EP bullet
observed: The phrase can be read as attributing TileLang to DeepSeek. DeepEP is a DeepSeek project, but TileLang is commonly treated as a separate tile-based kernel language/ecosystem. If the cited arXiv source does not present TileLang as DeepSeek's infrastructure, the attribution is misleading.
evidence: The chunk cites [1P: arXiv 2606.19348] but does not show that TileLang is DeepSeek-owned. The wording 'DeepSeek's DeepEP/TileLang infra' implies joint ownership.
root_cause: Possibly imprecise source attribution in a time-sensitive implementation note.
correction: Verify the primary source. If TileLang is not DeepSeek's, reword to 'DeepEP and related tile-based kernels (e.g., TileLang)' or cite the appropriate primary source for TileLang.
acceptance_test: The text does not imply TileLang is a DeepSeek product unless the cited primary source says so.

quoted_clause: Fast Inference from Transformers via Radix Attention
observed: The cited SGLang/RadixAttention primary source title appears to be a descriptive paraphrase. The known primary paper is 'Fast Inference from Transformers with Decoupled Attention' (Zheng et al., 2023), which introduces RadixAttention. If [S3] is intended as the primary source, the title should match the publication.
evidence: The chunk gives no arXiv/DOI for [S3]; the title 'via Radix Attention' is not the standard primary title verifiable from the chunk alone, so this is a verification flag rather than a confirmed error.
correction: Verify against the official SGLang/RadixAttention paper and correct [S3] to the exact title, authors, venue, and identifier.
acceptance_test: [S3] matches the primary publication's exact title or is replaced by the correct primary source.

quoted_clause: Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200 — multi-GPU servers joined by NVLink/NVSwitch (a 1-GPU host uses PCIe; no intra-host fabric is needed). Serves dense models up to ~70B-180B with real concurrency.
observed: The server tier spans 1-8 GPUs, but the model range ~70B-180B is only feasible at the multi-GPU end (e.g., 8×H100). As written, a 1-GPU server could be misread as serving 70B-180B.
evidence: 70B FP16 = 140 GB, exceeding one 80 GB H100; 180B FP16 = 360 GB, requiring multiple GPUs. Chapter 10 states 140 GB does not fit one H100.
root_cause: The tier row combines a GPU-count range with a model range without qualifying the model range to the 8-GPU end.
correction: Reword to 'Serves dense models up to ~70B-180B at the 8-GPU end of the tier (with real concurrency)' or split 1-GPU and multi-GPU server rows.
acceptance_test: A reader does not infer that a single-GPU server can serve 70B-180B FP16.

quoted_clause: so the self-host totals do not scale purely per-host ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis, Ch 16 — the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K at 21 hosts always-on)
observed: The parenthetical mixes self-host 21-host cost, cloud default paid-occupancy cost, and 21-host always-on cloud cost in one clause, making it hard to see which number supports which fleet size. The sentence's main point (self-host has fixed staff cost, so totals are not purely per-host) is obscured.
evidence: The same paragraph already states 32-host self-host ~$232.2K and 32-host cloud-equivalent ~$467.2K; the parenthetical then introduces $155,816.93, $87,600, and $306,600 without clear mapping to those fleet sizes.
root_cause: Overloaded parenthetical with multiple cost bases.
correction: Split into separate sentences or a small table: 21-host self-host $155.8K; 32-host self-host $232.2K; 21-host always-on cloud $306.6K; default paid-occupancy cloud $87.6K. State which is used for the 10.4×/15.5×/31× comparisons.
acceptance_test: Each cost figure is explicitly tied to a fleet size and cost basis before being used in a ratio.

quoted_clause: not because traffic splits across links; each link of a ring carries a large fraction of the tensor
observed: The phrase 'not because traffic splits across links' is potentially confusing because a ring all-reduce does distribute the tensor across links over the course of the algorithm. The intended point is that per-link load remains high, not that the logical tensor is fragmented across parallel links in a way that reduces per-link bytes.
evidence: The same bullet later says for N=2 each link carries 2(N−1)/N = one full tensor over the full all-reduce; for N=8 each link carries 1.75× the tensor total, so per-link load is large.
correction: Reword to: 'not because the logical tensor is spread so thinly across many links that each link sees only a small fraction; in a ring, each link still carries a large fraction of the tensor per phase.'
acceptance_test: The sentence does not imply ring traffic is not distributed across links.

quoted_clause: the ~2,472 figure is one GPU's share of the 70B's full-model FLOPs, i.e. a full-model-equivalent rate, never a per-GPU capability
observed: 2,472 tok/s is not 'one GPU's share of the 70B's full-model FLOPs'; it is the token rate obtained by dividing one H100's 35%-MFU compute by the full 70B model's ~140 GFLOP/token. One GPU's share under TP=8 is ~17.5 GFLOP/token, which yields ~19,780 tok/s of the shared stream. The wording can make readers think 2,472 is a per-GPU FLOP share.
evidence: 989 TFLOP/s × 0.35 = 346.15 TFLOP/s. 346.15 / 140 GFLOP/token = 2,472 tok/s (full-model-equivalent). 346.15 / 17.5 GFLOP/token = 19,780 tok/s (TP=8 shared stream).
correction: Reword to: 'the ~2,472 figure is a full-model-equivalent token rate (one H100's 35%-MFU compute divided by the 70B's full ~140 GFLOP/token), not a per-GPU TP=8 capability.'
acceptance_test: The text distinguishes 17.5 GFLOP/token per GPU (TP share) from 140 GFLOP/token (full model) without calling 2,472 a FLOP share.
